messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo Alvarez was 24 when he left the Army and returned to a junior financial analyst job in a glass office tower downtown, but he spoke about the deployment as if the most important part of him had been left there. In session he described one firefight in particular, during a patrol that moved through a wide, exposed stretch of road between damaged buildings. He remembered the brightness first, the flat openness, how visible they all were, and then the crack of gunfire and the chaos that followed. A man from his unit was hit. Mateo could recall certain moments with painful precision—the color of the dust on his friend’s uniform, the sound of someone shouting for cover, the feeling of his own hands moving too fast—yet the sequence would not hold together for him. He would start telling it and then get lost, unsure what came before what, with sharp fragments breaking in out of nowhere and disappearing before he could make sense of them.

What stayed with him most was not only that his friend died, but his conviction that he had become the kind of person he did not recognize. He had come to believe that in those minutes he had acted against his own values, and he returned home certain that something essential in him had been damaged. He said, in the flat, definite way he said many things, that he had no future worth picturing. Among college friends now building careers and dating and making plans, Mateo felt permanently set apart, as if everyone else had remained inside ordinary life while he had crossed into somewhere he could not come back from. That belief colored the way he held the memory itself: instead of settling into a story with a beginning and end, it remained a collection of brutally clear images that seemed to arrive charged with accusation, each piece seeming to confirm his sense that he was not the man he should have been.

In the months after discharge, those memories began intruding in ordinary places. At work, walking across the open trading floor toward a conference room, he would suddenly feel the same exposed vulnerability he had felt on that road overseas. A bright expanse of windows, the long distance between desks, even the empty atrium in the lobby could bring up a fragment—the dust, the shouting, the sight of his friend going down—so abruptly that he would stop mid-step and feel disoriented. Because the memories came in isolated, vivid pieces and never in an order he could control, he became increasingly determined not to give them any opening. He started taking narrower side corridors whenever he could, lingering by walls, choosing enclosed stairwells over the open lobby, and timing lunch to avoid the busiest common areas.

His view of himself pushed the avoidance further. Mateo was certain that if he spoke about what happened, other people would hear what he already believed about himself: that he had failed, that something shameful had been revealed in him, that he no longer belonged with people who had not done what he had done. He stopped his mother when she gently mentioned the soldier who had died. He ignored texts from a former squadmate who wanted to catch up. When coworkers asked routine questions about his military service, he gave clipped answers and changed the subject. Anything that reminded him of the man he lost—a memorial post online, a holiday honoring service members, even a song they used to play in the barracks—was quickly shut off or scrolled past. Avoiding those reminders felt like the only way to keep grief from breaking through and exposing how little future he believed he had.

Over time the pattern narrowed his life. At the office he was still technically competent, but colleagues noticed how often he declined team lunches held in the bright open plaza below the building, or how he positioned himself at the edge of meeting rooms nearest the door. Friends stopped inviting him out after he repeatedly refused. The less he talked and the more carefully he steered around reminders, the less chance he had to place the memory into any coherent order, and the more it returned as disconnected flashes. Each intrusion seemed to prove to him that he was stuck in the event and permanently outside everyone else’s world. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the effort of managing his days around what he could not see, hear, mention, or remember clearly. What finally brought him in was a morning at work when crossing the open floor triggered such a vivid fragment that he had to lock himself in a restroom stall until it passed. He said he was afraid that this was all his life would be from now on—avoiding, bracing, and keeping silent—but some part of him still hoped there might be a way to remember what happened without being condemned by it every time it returned.
